title: Have You Gone Grey So Young, Before the Morning of Old Age?
intro: In 2014 Ihab al-Shabatat posted these verses under the title “A Sigh after the First Grey Hair”, with notes of his own. The young man cannot tell whether this first white hair marks a dawn or a setting sun, though his heart still beats like wings. He traces his people's wounds across the earth before turning to his own grief and the strange forest where the dove and the lions can both be heard.

translation: Have you gone grey so young, before the morning of old age?
Is that the light of dawn coming, or my setting sun?
1.sharh: He finds the first grey hair and speaks to himself as “you”. When he calls it “my setting sun”, the white hair that could pass for dawn becomes a sign of his own passing.

translation: I never went unwillingly to face an adversary,
nor was my pounding heart forced to seem calm.
2.sharh: He claims the freedom both to face a quarrel and to keep his temper. The two almost identical words for constraint make the pulse beneath that composure audible.

translation: A bird flying high in the sky
is like my heart beating out on the steppes.
3.sharh: The beat of the heart finds its counterpart in the beat of a wing. The sky above the bird and the open country around the man give the movement room.

translation: Like basil that the winds caress,
offering up its scent at sunset,
4.sharh: The breeze brushes the plant and releases a fragrance it seems to give away. In Arabic, the words for basil, winds and scent all carry an echo of one another.

translation: like a drop of spring water in the meadows
that flies up as dew at the nightingale's song,
5.sharh: The drop takes flight at the bird's voice. The poet gives dew, which usually settles on the grass, the movement of the bird that sings above it.

translation: like a wave that rises far out at sea
and draws close to the desert sands,
6.sharh: The wave first appears on the distant water, then stands close against the sand. The eye can follow the whole journey from one half of the verse to the other.

translation: like a silent night spreading its hush,
so vast it lights the stars of other worlds.
7.sharh: Night lays silence over the scene and becomes the very thing that lights the stars. It prepares the claim that silence, too, can make something perceptible.

translation: Silence need not mean ignorance. At times
it speaks more eloquently than a master of words.
8.sharh: A quiet person may have more to convey than an accomplished speaker. The stars in the preceding line have already shown how much a silent night can disclose.

translation: Nor have I ever marvelled, as people suppose,
at the faults in the ways of those before us.
9.sharh: People mistake his interest in his predecessors' failings for astonishment. Their past matters to him because he can still see what it has left on the ground.

translation: Deaths strike the face of the earth,
and on it my people are the trace of scars.
10.sharh: The earth has a skin that can be struck. His people's presence is legible on it as the raised mark that outlasts a wound.

translation: Once she was like a radiant-faced maiden,
by your father's life, beyond reproach.
11.sharh: He remembers the same people in the figure of a young woman with a bright face. The oath makes her honour a matter to which he will personally testify.

translation: O sister of Aaron, who from the first
never seemed a stranger to calamity,
12.sharh: He addresses his people in words once addressed to Mary when she faced her accusers. The maiden of the preceding line has an innocence that adversity has already tested.

translation: did chargers range through the nights
so you could wash in a stranger's water?
13.sharh: Galloping horses suggest a night of exertion. The bitter outcome is the woman's dependence on someone else's water for so intimate an act as washing.

translation: Our tragedies are like a phoenix boasting
that its ash is the tailbone from which wars rise.
14.sharh: In the poet's own note, the little bone from which the body will rise again meets the phoenix that rises from its ashes. What returns to life here is war itself.

translation: From tender blood it sips our fragrance
and soars over the green of the paths.
15.sharh: The poet identifies the fragrance with children in his note. Their young blood feeds the bird, which flies on above green paths as if the scene below it were untroubled.

translation: At times it colours its feathers with water
drawn off by the deep shadows of pallor.
16.sharh: The phoenix dyes its plumage with a liquid drawn from faces drained of colour. The sheen of its feathers carries a cost that someone looking only at the bird could miss.

translation: Do not show me beauty in faces
whose loveliness leaves no trace in the heart.
17.sharh: After the terrible making of those bright feathers, a beautiful face alone has little to offer him. The poet links its appeal to the Quranic description of a brilliant colour that delights the eye.

translation: Life's mills pour out people,
and earth's wind turns with the grain.
18.sharh: The mills pour people out as a mill would pour out flour. A turning wind and countless grains give a physical scale to the succession of human lives.

translation: Night whispers that truth is pearls,
scattered, bearing witness in fresh blood.
19.sharh: Truth appears as separate shining pearls against fresh blood. The voice that points them out is a whisper after the great turning of the mills.

translation: Do not try to follow my tears with your eyes.
They have wandered off in all directions.
20.sharh: The woman he addresses cannot track the grief back to a single eye. The poet glosses the final word as sides or directions, so the tears seem to have gone everywhere.

translation: My worries shake the trunk of my innards,
and the corner of my eye pours and pours.
21.sharh: The worries shake him like a tree trunk, bringing tears down. The image recalls Mary shaking the palm for fruit and gives the earlier address to her a second echo.

translation: I never lost heart over the passing days, but
I saw my saddle dripping with my sins.
22.sharh: The distress belongs to what he is taking with him on the journey. The sins have soaked through even the saddle on which he travels.

translation: I walked with the darkness, pondering on
the heights of my longing for a sun still unseen.
23.sharh: He walks with night for company while his desire climbs towards a hidden sun. The division of the line suspends him briefly between darkness and those imagined heights.

translation: Will the world draw back a veil for me
and show the very substance of this feeble earth's past?
24.sharh: He wants access to what the earth has kept of its past, right down to its substance. The poet's gloss gives the closing adjective the sense of weakness or folly.

translation: I see people, doomed themselves, weeping for a soul,
as if the tears came from the dead one's equal.
25.sharh: The mourners seem already appointed to the fate they lament. The word for an equal makes the living and the dead counterparts even while one group weeps for the other.

translation: How often my God gives life to crumbling bones,
how often my God brings a physician to his end.
26.sharh: The physician who can keep others alive must also die, while God can restore life even to decaying remains. The repeated “how often” makes both events expressions of one power.

translation: A dove's cooing and the roar of lions
make the forest whole in this strange air.
27.sharh: The forest sounds complete only when tenderness and fierceness can be heard together. The bird's voice returns for the last line, now with the lions answering it.

1.1.1.head: شابَ
1.1.1.meaning: To go grey. The opening asks a young man whether his hair has already turned.

1.1.4-5.head: ضُحى المَشيب
1.1.4-5.meaning: “The morning of grey hair” gives old age an hour of the day of its own.

1.2.5.head: مَغيب
1.2.5.meaning: Sunset, here the speaker's own going down.

2.1.2.head: كُره
2.1.2.meaning: Reluctance or hardship. Changing the first vowel in the next half brings out the sense of compulsion.

3.2.5.head: السُّهوب
3.2.5.meaning: Broad stretches of open, level country.

4.1.1.head: رَيحان
4.1.1.meaning: Basil, or a fragrant herb more generally.

5.2.4.head: العَندَليب
5.2.4.meaning: A nightingale, celebrated for its song.

7.2.4.head: رَحيب
7.2.4.meaning: Spacious, stretching far in every direction.

9.2.1.head: خِصال
9.2.1.meaning: Traits of character, habits for which someone is known.

10.1.1-2.head: أَديم الأَرض
10.1.1-2.meaning: “The earth's skin” is its surface, imagined here as a face that can be scarred.

10.1.4.meaning: Deaths, or the fates that bring them.

11.1.4.head: صَبوح
11.1.4.meaning: Bright-faced and lovely to look at.

11.2.1-2.meaning: “By your father's life” is an oath.

12.1.3-4.head: أُخت هارون
12.1.3-4.meaning: “Sister of Aaron” is how Mary is addressed when she brings her child to her people in Quran 19.28.

13.1.4.head: عادِيات
13.1.4.meaning: Galloping horses, a term that also opens Quran 100.

14.1.2.head: عَنقاء
14.1.2.meaning: Anqa', a fabulous bird cast here as the phoenix rising from its ashes.

14.2.3.head: عَجب
14.2.3.meaning: The small bone at the base of the spine. A hadith says that from it the body will be put together again at the resurrection.

15.1.3.head: غَضيض
15.1.3.meaning: Fresh and tender, as of something newly grown.

15.1.5.head: شَذى
15.1.5.meaning: Fragrance, also the small pieces of aromatic wood used as perfume. The poet says the image stands for children here.

16.2.2.head: دَياجير
16.2.2.meaning: Depths of darkness, used here of pallor so intense it seems to have dark recesses.

17.2.3.head: بانَ
17.2.3.meaning: To show itself, to be discernible.

19.2.4.head: رَطيب
19.2.4.meaning: Still wet, said of blood newly shed.

20.2.5.head: الجُنوب
20.2.5.meaning: Sides or directions, the plural of janb in the poet's gloss.

21.1.2.head: جِذع
21.1.2.meaning: A tree trunk. The shaking recalls Mary and the palm tree in Quran 19.25.

21.2.1-2.head: مُؤق العَين
21.2.1-2.meaning: “The inner corner of the eye”, beside the nose, where tears collect.

22.2.2.head: الرَّحل
22.2.2.meaning: A camel saddle, and by extension the gear carried on a journey.

24.2.1.head: كُنه
24.2.1.meaning: The essence of a thing, its innermost nature.

24.2.4.head: اللَّغوب
24.2.4.meaning: Feeble or foolish in the poet's own gloss. A different vocalisation of the same letters means weariness.

26.1.5.head: رَميم
26.1.5.meaning: What has decayed and crumbled, especially bone.

27.2.2.head: الغاب
27.2.2.meaning: A dense wood or thicket where wild animals shelter.
